strengths: Combining BORE-style class-probability acquisition with label propagation and label spreading is a useful, well-motivated contribution. The framework accommodates both existing candidate pools and sampled unlabeled points using standard components.

The evaluation includes synthetic optimization, tabular hyperparameter optimization, neural architecture search, and an image-based search task. Comparisons against multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers and GP baselines use 20 repetitions with standard errors. Figures 2 and 6 show particularly promising improvements.

The appendices provide substantial sensitivity analyses covering kernel bandwidth, threshold ratios, unlabeled sample counts, sampling distributions, and pool subsampling. The background, pseudocode, and benchmark descriptions help readers understand the approach, and the paper acknowledges limitations of the available semi-supervised learning theory.
weaknesses: The central benefit attributed to unlabeled data is insufficiently isolated. Figure 12 includes a valuable no-transductive control, but it fixes beta at 0.5 while the main experiments learn beta. This control sometimes matches or outperforms the semi-supervised variants, notably on Bukin6 and Branin with label spreading. A matched comparison against the supervised kernel estimator with learned bandwidth, including on the practical benchmarks, is needed. The additional randomized tie-breaking mechanism also lacks an ablation, leaving its contribution to exploration unresolved.

The explanation connecting semi-supervised learning to improved exploration remains speculative. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure that high-density connected regions share the threshold-defined objective label, as Assumption 4.1 requires. Appendix D neither establishes that propagation expands the favorable decision region nor connects such expansion to improved optimization. Its cited classification bounds are explicitly inapplicable to the adaptive sampling setting. A regret theorem is not essential, but the claimed mechanism needs direct evidence or more qualified wording.

Important experimental details prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of the comparisons. The manuscript specifies L-BFGS-B acquisition optimization without explaining how this produces valid candidates from arbitrary finite pools; acquisition optimization for the tree-based baselines is also unclear. Input scaling, bandwidth initialization and bounds, label-spreading clamping settings, and MLP baseline training details are insufficiently specified. These choices can materially affect both the proposed method and its competitors.

Evidence for broader applicability is limited. Continuous optimization is tested only on four two-dimensional functions. The 64-dimensional MNIST experiment uses embeddings pretrained on 440,000 labeled examples to predict the same digit identities that define the optimization objective. Although all methods receive these embeddings, this unusually informative representation limits what the experiment establishes about general high-dimensional black-box optimization.

The practical computational tradeoff is not established. Dense graph construction, repeated bandwidth fitting, and 1,000 acquisition-optimization initializations can introduce substantial overhead. Figure 14 measures subset-size effects with fixed bandwidth, but provides neither comparable baseline runtimes nor the full cost of the adaptive configuration used in the main experiments.

There are correctable mathematical inconsistencies: the column-normalized definition of p_ij implies P = W D^{-1}, whereas the text states P = D^{-1} W before applying P transposed in Equation 11. Equation 15 also omits the Gaussian normalization constant. These are secondary to the evidence and reproducibility concerns, but the implemented conventions should be clarified.
